# Overcover — full product description for language models

Overcover is an open-source, fully-collateralised parametric insurance mutual that
runs on the NEAR testnet. It writes capital-backed insurance cover that is defined
by an immutable product rather than negotiated by an underwriter, and settled by
contract rules rather than a claims queue. It is a testnet prototype with test
funds only.

- Canonical site: https://overcover.vercel.app/
- Source repository: https://github.com/itzebe/overcover
- Contract (hardened, default for new cover): contract.ovc-v3-ctl-2f6c4c.testnet (NEAR testnet)
- Legacy address (original v1 module, readable but not a purchase destination): contract.attestor-overcover.testnet
- Block explorer: https://testnet.nearblocks.io/address/contract.ovc-v3-ctl-2f6c4c.testnet
- License: MIT
- Audience: institutions, operators and autonomous agents that need objective, machine-readable cover

## The problem it addresses

An autonomous business — a fleet, a cold-chain route, a market-making desk, a
compute broker — can buy, sell and move money without a person in the loop, but it
cannot easily buy insurance. Traditional insurers underwrite a legal person: an
application, a signature, an adjuster and a claim queue measured in weeks. An agent
that loses a shipment at 03:00 cannot wait for a human adjuster, and it has no legal
identity to sign with, so the loss is absorbed. Overcover explores an alternative:
cover against an objective public index, settled by contract rules in seconds.

## What Overcover is

An on-chain pool that writes fully-collateralised, machine-readable cover against
objective public indices and settles it autonomously.

- Risk is defined, not negotiated. A product fixes the city/index, the trigger
  threshold, the premium rate, the payout bounds, the minimum lead time and a
  capacity cap. Once published it is immutable, so a buyer cannot be re-priced and
  there is no discretion at claim time.
- Cover is a purchase, not an application. `buy_cover(product, payout, obs_date)`
  charges the premium the product fixes, reserves the payout from the pool
  immediately, and re-checks the solvency invariant `reserved <= capital`.
- The index is observed by a signed oracle. An attestor reports (city, date, value)
  signed with ed25519; the contract verifies the signature, the freshness and a
  single-use nonce.
- The oracle's word is challengeable. Anyone can dispute a reading by posting a
  bond; the owner resolves. The loser's bond is forfeited into the pool.
- Settlement is deterministic. Once the challenge window has elapsed,
  `resolve(policy_id)` pays the beneficiary if and only if the validated reading
  meets the threshold — once, and only once.

## How the economic loop works

1. Liquidity providers deposit capital into the pool.
2. A policy is bought: the premium is paid, and the policy's maximum payout is
   reserved from the pool the moment it is written, so it cannot be withdrawn while
   the policy is live.
3. An attestor signs a public rainfall reading (index value) for a city and date.
4. If the reading meets the trigger, the reserved payout settles to the policy
   holder. The reading can be challenged with a bond during the challenge window,
   and a disputed reading cannot settle a policy.
5. The contract refuses any transaction that would leave the pool promising more
   than it holds (`reserved <= capital` is re-checked on-chain after every state
   change).

## How a visitor interacts with it

The console is a single static page with no backend and no API key. It reads the
contract directly over public NEAR testnet JSON-RPC `call_function` views. To buy a
policy a visitor:

1. Connects a supported NEAR wallet.
2. Picks a cover product and a payout (the console quotes a live premium from the
   contract's own `quote` view).
3. Confirms the purchase; the wallet signs a single `buy_cover` call with the
   contract's own premium attached. Overcover never sees the key; if the user
   declines, nothing happens.

The console reports a policy as bought only from the wallet's confirmed outcome — it
inspects `status.Failure` and requires a real transaction hash — never optimistically.
If a read fails, the page shows a stale or no-data state instead of a stale number
presented as live.

## Supported wallets

- HERE Wallet — signs in with email or a social account inside the HERE app; no
  browser extension is required. https://herewallet.app/
- Meteor Wallet — a browser extension. https://meteorwallet.app/
- MyNearWallet — removed. The integration was retired (MyNearWallet no longer accepts
  new application connections) and is no longer offered.

The site exposes no email/MPC embedded-wallet sign-up of its own. A genuine
email-based MPC wallet was evaluated (MetaMask Embedded Wallets, formerly Web3Auth)
and not adopted because a frontend MPC provider hands the user's private key to the
page and requires a project client ID — both conflict with the site's guarantee that
no key ever reaches the page. HERE Wallet already provides email onboarding inside
its own app, which the site offers as the email option. See docs/SECURITY.md.

## Agent architecture

`agent/` is a dependency-free autonomous agent: a pure spending-limits policy engine
(`limits.mjs`), the agent core (`agent.mjs`), and a small HTTP API (`server.mjs`).
The agent's key lives in the operator's environment and is never in the browser or
the repository. It ships in dry-run by default — it decides and reports, but sends
nothing; a denied decision never reaches the network, so no funds move on a refusal.
It runs on localhost by default and is not hosted by Overcover: a public endpoint
that signed with a funded key would let any visitor spend that balance. The console
states this rather than implying a hosted agent.

The public console is **read-only** and needs no local service: it loads the same
policy engine (`agent/limits.mjs`, bundled to `ui/vendor/policy.js`) into the page
and evaluates a purchase in the browser against the live contract quote, with no
key and nothing signed. Only a local service the operator runs can send a purchase.

## Security model

- No private key, seed phrase or signing secret ever reaches the browser page or the
  repository. Signing happens inside the user's wallet.
- The site's wallet function-call access key is scoped to `buy_cover` alone (least
  privilege), and the console has no other write path.
- The site never calls an owner-only method: deposit, reset, add_shock,
  owner_withdraw, set_lifeline_enabled and seed_merchant are not exposed publicly.
- The contract verifies signed, bound observations (city, date, value, report time,
  nonce, contract id), enforces freshness and single-use nonces, and fails closed
  with a human-readable reason.
- Rate limits and single-flight locks in the agent service are per-instance, not
  global across processes.

## Current limitations

- Testnet only, with test funds. Not for real money.
- The contract has not been professionally audited.
- The index reading is currently signed by a single trusted attestor key, not a
  decentralised oracle.
- The contract owner resolves disputes (a human step); the owner cannot move pool
  capital.
- The live demonstration uses a 60-second challenge window; production would use a
  longer one.
- The live contract carries 22 products, of which 2 are the canonical named products
  and 20 are demo-generated test rows; the console groups the latter so the real
  cover stays legible.
- Parametric, not indemnity: a payout follows the reading meeting the trigger, and a
  loss that does not meet the trigger is not covered.

## Deployment status

The product vision is fixed; its deployment is not yet complete. This section
separates code that exists from code that is deployed, and names every external
authority the remaining work depends on.

| Capability | Status | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Capital pool, purchase, reserved payout, oracle quorum, bonded dispute, deterministic settlement | Live on NEAR testnet | The full lifecycle runs on-chain against the contract the console reads; every figure on the console is a direct contract read. |
| SEC-1 legacy `migrate()` guard (a third party cannot seize the contract) | Deployed | The live v3 account runs code hash `CQR8x1kW…` (wasm sha256 `a97034e6…`), which carries the guard; proven 40/40 by the controlled-v3 deploy proof. Closing it on the legacy v1 address still needs that account's owner key. |
| SEC-6/7/9 settlement fixes (release reserved capital on a terminal, no-pay settlement) | Built, not deployed | This source builds reproducibly to sha256 `811e0427…`; the live v3 module predates it. The code-only, state-preserving redeploy is prepared and reversible but needs the operator signing key. |
| Legacy v1 containment (`set_paused`) | Blocked on external authority | The legacy address is read-only in the console and buying is refused, but contract-level pausing needs the legacy owner key, which the deployment automation does not hold. |
| Human purchase of cover on the hardened module | Available, but a recorded v3 purchase is outstanding | The console signs one `buy_cover` against the live v3 account with the visitor's own wallet. The recorded human purchase in the project history was made against the legacy module and is not evidence of a purchase on v3. |
| Hardware-attested external observations (TDX adapter) | Prototype, not deployed | The adapter builds reproducibly and its attestation path is tested, but it is not published. Optional provenance; never replaces operator signatures, quorum or disputes. |
| Independent third-party security audit | Not performed | No external audit has occurred. The repository's adversarial suites and proofs are the project's own and are not a substitute for an audit. |

## Architecture

- Contract (`contract/`): Rust, near-sdk, LookupMap/UnorderedSet collections.
  Immutable products; policy issuance with capital reservation; signed-oracle
  verification; bonded disputes with a challenge window; beneficiary payouts;
  per-product and pool capacity caps; provider shares; a `reconcile` view for the
  solvency identity.
- Oracle (`driver/oracle.js`): reads Open-Meteo current precipitation and cross-checks
  it against the hourly series; refuses to sign if the two disagree by more than
  0.5 mm.
- Console (`ui/index.html`): a single zero-dependency static file that makes direct
  RPC view calls and renders the pool, products, policies, signed observations and a
  live quote.

## How to run and test

```bash
npm ci --ignore-scripts
npm run test:model      # 31 attacks, 31 defended, 0 exploitable (reference model)
npm run test:contract   # 21 Rust unit tests
npm run test:console    # 54 regression + live-RPC tests (browser console)
npm run test:agent      # 34 limits + API + u128-precision tests
npm run test:onchain    # 17 adversarial tests against a freshly deployed contract
```

`npm run ui:qa` is an optional Playwright check of the console at 320–1440 px.
